prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing optical time standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks fit the committee's mandate as I read it: an invention, with an identifiable original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping proposal of 2001-2003 and the first strontium lattice-clock demonstrations) followed by the experimental realisation that took the concept to the 10^-18 level (Ye and JILA). It is experimentally verified many times over, in several laboratories and with several species, and it is a tool that opens a door: gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, searches for variation of constants and for dark matter, relativistic geodesy and a prospective redefinition of the second. The credited pair is clean and distinct, which is rare on this shortlist, and seven of eight members ranked it, three of them first. That breadth of support matters to me less than the fact that the attribution can be defended from the historical record.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is one of framing and novelty: the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-trapping prize already honoured neighbouring parts of optical metrology, so a sceptic can call this the more elegant successor to recognised work, which is exactly what the Physics Prize is not supposed to reward. A second problem is priority within the lattice-clock lineage (Katori versus Ye, and the contributions of Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others who are not credited). Finally, a redefinition of the second is pending, and one can argue that the full consequences of the invention have not yet been realised.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because the magic-wavelength idea is simple, original and decisive, and he sees the two-person credit as Katori's concept plus Ye's push to record accuracy; he worries that overlap with the comb prize could make the committee cautious.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and I want to be explicit about the overlap worry rather than dismiss it. The comb prize of 2005 recognised a way of counting optical cycles; it did not recognise trapping neutral atoms so that the light shift cancels. The lattice clock is a different invention that uses the comb as one component, in the same way that many prize-winning instruments use earlier prizewinning tools. I would, however, ask the committee to keep the citation about the magic-wavelength lattice and not drift into a general award for precision timekeeping, which would revive the lifetime-achievement flavour I wish to avoid.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube first and lattice clocks second, notes that the individual roles within IceCube rest on memory, and says he would rely on AMO colleagues for priority between Katori and Ye's group.
responses.response: I take his deference seriously and will try to supply the AMO-side judgement I can: priority for the concept is Katori's, and priority for taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier is Ye's, so the pair is not an arbitrary compromise. On IceCube I am sympathetic, since I ranked it second for the same new-window reason, but my disagreement is about attribution. Pearce himself concedes that the Halzen-Karle pair is a compromise within a collaboration of hundreds, and Yoshida and the AMANDA pioneers are not settled either. I am not yet absolutely sure we have found the people who did the original work, and for me that is the decisive difference from the clocks.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clean case of a basic quantum phenomenon becoming a platform, but ranks optical lattice clocks only sixth, citing overlap with earlier metrology prizes.
responses.response: I respect his case for circuit QED, but I would qualify it on timing and scope: the 2025 prize already went to macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, and four names are credited where at most three can be taken, so Girvin or Blais must be dropped on a judgement call I find uncomfortable. On the metrology overlap I disagree for the reason I gave to Kroll: the 2005 and 2012 prizes concern different inventions. If the committee truly feels that the hardware family has been honoured enough, that argues for the clocks as much as against them, since optical clocks have not been recognised at all.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clocks first on the grounds that the idea is simple and original, but asks whether the committee would see it as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the precision-timekeeping line already honoured, and notes that Ye's scope could be contested.
responses.response: I think it is distinct, and the test I would apply is whether the achievement could be stated without leaning on the earlier prizes: trapping atoms at the magic wavelength so that the lattice does not perturb the clock transition is such a statement. On Ye's scope, I would keep the citation narrow, naming lattice clocks only, and leave his comb and molecule work out of it. That also answers her question about fairness to Hall and Hansch, who are already laureates.

uncertainties: Exact historical priority between Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and early demonstrations versus related work in Lemonde's and Hollberg's groups, which should be checked against the primary literature.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second, or whether the invention is already mature enough.
Whether a narrow citation is sufficient or the credited pair should be broadened, since Takamoto and others realised the first lattice clock with Katori.
Whether the IceCube attribution (Halzen, Karle, Yoshida) can be settled convincingly enough to compete with a cleaner two-person case.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the optical lattice clock candidate. I note only that committee colleague Goran Johansson is at Chalmers Physics with me, and that he ranks circuit QED first; I do not think this requires recusal on any shortlisted candidate. I have no known collaboration with the credited persons.
